entry.evidence: detailed studies including ore paragenesis, host rocks geochemistry, and ore formation in the Rangpo area have not been carried out

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the Rangpo polymetallic deposit in metasedimentary host rocks formed, and in what tectonic setting its host rocks were deposited.
steps.quote: The present work attempts to investigate the formation of polymetallic deposit hosted within metasedimentary rocks in Rangpo

steps.action: The authors take from Sarkar et al. (2000) a Pb-Pb age of 1,800 Ma for the Rangpo ores and use it as a premise.
steps.quote: investigated Pb–Pb isotope systematics and assigned an age of 1,800 Ma to the Rangpo ores

steps.action: The authors describe the field occurrence of the mineralization, the host-rock petrography, and the ore microscopy (reflected and transmitted light) of the primary and secondary ore minerals and their textures.
steps.quote: Chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite, sphalerite, and cobaltite appear to be coeval as shown by their mutual boundaries

steps.action: From the textural relations (coeval grains, exsolution, replacement, alteration), the authors infer a three-stage paragenetic sequence.
steps.quote: Three stages of ore formation are established for the Rangpo polymetallic deposit

steps.action: The authors measure major, trace, and REE contents of 14 host-rock samples by WD-XRF and ICP-MS and plot the major oxides on Harker diagrams.
steps.quote: show a negative correlation of SiO2 with Al2O3, MgO, K2O, and TiO2

steps.action: The authors run reference standards with the XRF and ICP-MS analyses and report precision and accuracy (reported in the analytical-techniques section).
steps.quote: The standard samples SGR-1, SCO-1, G2, and JG2 were used in the analysis.

steps.action: The authors compare the host-rock data with published classification and discrimination fields: Herron 1988; Roser & Korsch 1986 K2O/Na2O-SiO2; CIA; Mg#-SiO2; McLennan et al. 1993 Th/Sc-Zr/Sc; La/Sc-Th/Co. They also use the smooth REE patterns to argue that the REEs were not affected by metamorphism.
steps.quote: mostly in the passive margin field but a few in the active continental margin/arc setting

steps.action: The authors use SEM-BSE imaging with EDX spot analyses and line scans as a second method to confirm the mineral phases and textures identified by ore microscopy.
steps.quote: confirmed the mineral phases and has provided textural and composition information

steps.action: The authors measure the mineral chemistry of sphalerite, galena, chalcopyrite, and pyrite by EPMA and report stoichiometry and minor and trace elements.
steps.quote: Sphalerite consists of high Fe, which varies from 7.14 to 7.92 wt%.

steps.action: The authors calibrate the EPMA on natural and synthetic standards and give precision from repeated analysis of those standards (reported in the analytical-techniques section).
steps.quote: The precision of the instrument is almost 1% for major elements and up to 5% for the trace elements

steps.action: The authors set up two alternatives for the host sediments: recycled passive-margin sediment, or sediment with arc-derived or mafic input from an active margin.
steps.quote: the possibility of mixing of even arc-derived sediments from active margin cannot be ruled out

steps.action: The authors weigh their geochemical evidence against published Himalayan records of a ~1,800-1,830 Ma active arc and the 1,800 Ma Pb-Pb age of the Rangpo ores.
steps.quote: considering earlier studies carried out elsewhere in Himalaya

steps.action: The authors keep the interpretation of passive-margin deposition with an influx of magmatic material from an active continental arc during sedimentation.
steps.quote: the magmatic material was also derived from an active continental arc setting during the time of sedimentation

steps.action: From the restriction of the ores to the formation, the dissemination of ore along the foliation, and the deformation textures, the authors infer stratabound, pre-deformation mineralization.
steps.quote: the mineralization is strata bound, pre-deformation stage

steps.action: The authors compare the stage-I and stage-II assemblage (magnetite-sulphide, arsenopyrite-pyrrhotite, native Bi) with published high-temperature associations.
steps.quote: point to the high temperature of the ore formation

steps.action: Using the metamorphic overprint on the ores, read together with published Sikkim metamorphic studies, the authors infer that the mineralization is pre-Himalayan.
steps.quote: it can be suggested that the Rangpo ore mineralization is primarily pre-Himalayan

steps.action: The authors compare the EPMA chemistry of sphalerite with published ranges: the Fe-Zn inverse relation and high Fe as a temperature signal, Fe and Mn as magmatic-hydrothermal, Cr as a mafic link, and Zn/Cd against Mississippi Valley type versus exhalative systems.
steps.quote: these values are in the range of the exhalative system

steps.action: The authors keep the interpretation of a magmatic-fluid-driven ore system linking the active arc with the passive-margin setting in the Proterozoic.
steps.quote: it would be appropriate to foresee that the ore system in host metasedimentary rocks was developed

steps.action: The authors compare Co, Ni, and Ag in chalcopyrite and pyrite (inconclusive) and Ag and Sb in galena (high temperature, after George et al. 2016) with published genetic indicators.
steps.quote: Such high concentrations of Ag and Sb suggest that galena was formed at a high temperature

steps.action: The authors conclude that the ores formed at high temperature where mafic arc material was amalgamated with felsic-sourced passive-margin sediments.
steps.quote: the Rangpo ore mineralization was formed in a high-temperature environment, in the amalgamation of mafic material from the active arc

tree.answer: Polymetallic Cu-Pb-Zn sulphide ores in Proterozoic Gorubathan Formation metasediments at Rangpo
No; ore formation is known only from mineral textures and chemistry (traces)
Reconstruct the ore-forming conditions and the host-rock tectonic and provenance setting
Loosely: passive margin vs arc input; Mississippi Valley type vs exhalative; magmatic vs sedimentary Co/Ni signals
Partly; published discrimination fields and element ranges differ between settings
Conditions found in rock traces, not set
Weakly; standards and a second imaging method only, no robustness or independent data
Kept as best explanation: high-temperature ores with arc-derived mafic input into passive-margin sediments

end.claim: The Rangpo ore mineralization formed at high temperature in an environment where mafic mantle material from an active arc was amalgamated with passive-margin sediments derived from felsic sources.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the host-rock geochemistry with published tectonic discrimination fields (ore-bearing samples falling in the arc/active-margin and mantle-melt fields) and the EPMA mineral chemistry with published temperature indicators produced both halves of the claim.

gates.evidence: Sampling and analyses were descriptive and were not directed by a stated hypothesis (p. 5065). The data could have plotted in other discrimination fields, but no rival was set up for a decisive test, and the authors admit several indicators are 'not highly conclusive' (p. 5078). No thresholds or hypotheses were fixed beforehand.

imports.item: SEM-EDX and electron probe microanalysis (CAMECA SX-Five)
WD-XRF and ICP-MS with acid digestion

novelty_claims.quote: detailed studies including ore paragenesis, host rocks geochemistry, and ore formation in the Rangpo area have not been carried out
The present work is a new insight to understand the formation

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, although the paper acknowledges comments from the editor and three reviewers (p. 5080), so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: the three-stage paragenesis (best_explanation, from textures, p. 5067); pre-Himalayan, stratabound mineralization (best_explanation, p. 5077); the exhalative-type Zn/Cd signal, based on five analyses (best_explanation, weak; the authors say Cd isotopes would be more convincing, p. 5079); the Co/Ni genetic signal (none; 'difficult to pinpoint', p. 5079). Temperature is inferred only qualitatively; no geothermometer is applied. Sample counts are small (14 whole-rock samples; about 10 analyses per mineral), and the selection criteria for 'representative' samples are not given. Data are available only on request (p. 5080). The rivals are stated implicitly, as fields in discrimination diagrams, rather than as hypotheses tested before the data (inference).

disagreements.target: Workers arguing that amphibolite or granulite grade metamorphism mobilizes elements (Barovich & Patchett 1992; Pearce 1996; Tarney & Weaver 1987; [...]
disagreements.support: The authors side with those who find elemental mobility insignificant, and argue from smooth REE patterns with a uniform Eu anomaly that the REEs were not affected by metamorphism.
disagreements.quote: however many others believe that such elemental mobility remains insignificant

alternatives_considered.chosen: Relatively immobile elements (Sc, Zr, Nb, Hf, Al2O3, REE, Th, La) as provenance indicators
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Large-ion lithophile elements Rb, Sr, Ba
alternatives_considered.reason: Rb, Sr and Ba are highly mobile during metamorphism and secondary processes

alternatives_considered.chosen: EPMA quantitative mineral chemistry for interpretation
alternatives_considered.reason: SEM-EDX gave only a broad idea of the elements present

alternatives_considered.chosen: Qualitative reading of high Fe in sphalerite as high temperature
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Precise sphalerite geothermometry using Fe-rich patches, matrix and mole % FeS

alternatives_considered.chosen: Zn/Cd ratios in sphalerite to classify the ore system
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Zn/Cd combined with Cd isotope compositions
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (the authors note the combined approach is more convincing)
